In my own words I have repeatedly contrasted an “open society” with what I called a “closed society” – the latter being one in which the mass media are reduced to a “constant drone of sycophantic support for a particular orthodox political philosophy”【S2】. I argued that Singapore’s institutions were deliberately designed to avoid that closed‑society drift, insisting that “the fabric of a democratic society … allows for the free play of ideas … within the constitutional framework”【S2】.  

Nevertheless, I have also warned that “repression can only go up to a point” and that unchecked coercion would eventually turn the instruments of the state against its masters【S2】. In practice, I have maintained that open debate must be managed so that it does not destabilise the nation; the government therefore regulates media and public discourse to keep the debate “within the constitutional framework” while still permitting “novel, unorthodox … ideas” to be aired【S2】.  

Observers note that this approach has led some to describe Singapore as “semi‑authoritarian” or a “nanny state,” reflecting the tension between the desire for open debate and the pragmatic limits I have set on it【S3】.

I have always been asked whether Singapore is an “open” or a “closed” society, and the answer, if you wish to be precise, is that it is both – and that the balance between the two has been the very engine of our success.

When I speak of openness, I refer first and foremost to the openness of our economy. From the moment we opened our ports in the early 1960s, we invited foreign capital, technology and talent to come in, we built world‑class infrastructure, we cultivated a legal system that is transparent and predictable, and we have allowed our people to enjoy a standard of living that few could have imagined for a tiny island with no natural resources. In that sense Singapore is as open as any city‑state can be.

Politically, however, we have taken a different, more measured line. A society that is truly open in the Western sense – where any and every view can be aired at any time, where the loudest voice invariably wins, where the market of ideas is left to its own devices – is not always compatible with the realities of a multi‑racial, multi‑religious community that is only a few million strong. Our priority has always been to preserve social cohesion, to prevent the kind of sectarian strife that has plagued many larger nations. To that end we have set clear boundaries on public discourse: speech that incites racial or religious hatred, that threatens public order, or that undermines the very institutions that keep our society stable, is not tolerated.

That does not mean that debate is absent. On the contrary, I have always encouraged vigorous discussion within the parameters of responsibility. Ministers are expected to be questioned in Parliament; civil servants are urged to offer dissenting views in private; academics and journalists enjoy a degree of freedom that is uncommon in many of our neighbours. The key is that the debate occurs in a manner that is constructive, fact‑based, and respectful of the social compact we have all signed.

Open debate, in my view, is a tool – not an end in itself. It is valuable when it improves policy, sharpens our institutions, and helps us adapt to new challenges. It becomes counter‑productive when it devolves into partisan bickering, populist pandering, or the spread of misinformation that can erode trust among our peoples. Therefore, we have cultivated a culture where ideas are aired, but where the ultimate decision‑making rests on merit, long‑term vision, and the collective good.

In short, Singapore is open where openness serves the national interest – in trade, in education, in the free flow of capital and talent – and it is prudently circumscribed where unbridled freedom could jeopardise the fragile harmony that underpins our success. Open debate thrives within those limits, and it is precisely that calibrated openness that has allowed us to transform a small, resource‑poor island into a thriving, modern nation.

In my view, a fledgling nation cannot afford a press that merely critiques for its own sake. The mass media should act as a conduit that “present[s] Singapore’s problems simply and clearly and then explain how, if they support certain programmes and policies, these problems can be solved” [S1]. Its chief task is to reinforce the cultural values and social attitudes that our schools and universities are inculcating, not to undermine them [S1]. Consequently, freedom of the press must be “subordinated to the overriding needs of the integrity of Singapore, and to the primacy of purpose of an elected government” [S1]. We may allow foreign journalists to report facts, but we will not permit them to become “invigilator, adversary and inquisitor of the administration” as they might be elsewhere [S3]. In short, the media’s role is to educate, support and legitimize the nation‑building agenda, while remaining aligned with the government’s overarching objectives.

In my experience, the mass media is not a luxury for a fledgling nation; it is a cornerstone of nation‑building. When I set out to transform Singapore from a struggling port into a thriving metropolis, I learned that the press must serve three essential purposes.

**1. Convey a clear, coherent national narrative.**  
A new country is, by definition, a work in progress. Its people need to understand where we are headed, why we are taking certain steps, and what sacrifices may be required. The media should articulate the government’s vision in a way that is honest yet purposeful, so that citizens can rally behind a common goal rather than be swayed by rumors or foreign propaganda.

**2. Promote responsible citizenship and social cohesion.**  
Diversity is a strength, but it can also be a source of division if left unchecked. The press must highlight stories that bind us—our shared values, our collective achievements, and the challenges we face together. At the same time, it should discourage sensationalism that pits one community against another. In Singapore we instituted a “social responsibility” clause for broadcasters; a new nation would do well to adopt a similar principle, encouraging journalists to think of the long‑term health of the polity rather than short‑term headlines.

**3. Serve as a constructive check on power, within limits.**  
A free press is indispensable for accountability, but freedom without responsibility can become anarchy. The media should be free to expose genuine corruption, inefficiency, or abuse, but it must also respect the delicate balance of a young state that is still consolidating its institutions. In practice this means a regulatory framework that protects editorial independence while preventing the spread of falsehoods that could destabilise the nation.

In short, the mass media in a new country should be a disciplined partner of the state: a conduit for the national story, a promoter of unity, and a vigilant yet prudent watchdog. When these roles are fulfilled, the press becomes an engine of progress rather than a source of discord.

When I said “the cure for all this talk is really a good dose of incompetent government,” I was warning that an opposition‑led or poorly run administration would be a self‑inflicted remedy for the criticism we hear. In my view, an incompetent government would quickly unravel Singapore’s hard‑won stability – “you’ll never put Singapore together again, Humpty Dumpty cannot be put together again” – and the resulting chaos would be far worse than any political debate we face【S1】. In short, I meant that the alternative to strong, capable governance is not merely undesirable but potentially catastrophic for our nation’s prosperity and social order【S2】.

When I said that a government needs “a good dose of incompetence,” I was not praising mediocrity for its own sake. I was pointing to a practical reality that I observed while building Singapore from a tiny port city into a thriving nation‑state.

In the early 1960s we were faced with a choice. We could either create a bureaucracy that believed it could solve every problem perfectly, or we could accept that the machinery of government would, inevitably, make mistakes, over‑reach, and become complacent. The former path, I have always warned, leads to a leviathan that thinks it is infallible; the latter, if managed wisely, keeps the state humble and vigilant.

A “good dose of incompetence” therefore means:

1. **Built‑in humility.** When officials know that they are not omniscient, they are more likely to listen to dissenting voices, to seek expert advice, and to test policies on a small scale before rolling them out nationwide. In Singapore we instituted pilot projects, trial runs, and rigorous post‑mortems precisely because we accepted that we would get some things wrong.

2. **Checks on power.** If a government believes it can do everything flawlessly, it tends to concentrate authority and suppress criticism. A modest amount of failure forces the system to develop safeguards—parliamentary oversight, an independent civil service, a free press—so that errors are exposed and corrected.

3. **Motivation for improvement.** When a ministry’s programme flops, the embarrassment spurs reform. We learned, for instance, that the early attempts at public housing allocation were riddled with inefficiencies; the resulting public outcry pushed us to create the Housing Development Board, which later became a model of effectiveness.

4. **Public confidence through transparency.** Singaporeans have always been told that the government is not a deity but a servant. By openly acknowledging mistakes—whether in the 1975 water crisis or the 1997 Asian financial turbulence—we earned a degree of trust that could not have been achieved by a façade of perfection.

Let me be clear: the “dose” must be modest, never so large that the state becomes a disaster. The goal is a government that is competent enough to deliver essential services—clean water, safe housing, reliable transport—while remaining aware of its own limits. In that balance lies the resilience that has allowed Singapore to survive wars, economic shocks, and social upheavals.

So, when I invoked the phrase, I was urging leaders to cultivate a culture where competence is prized, but where a little measured incompetence is tolerated as a catalyst for vigilance, reform, and ultimately, better governance.

Singapore’s exit was not a voluntary “choice” but the result of a political and communal impasse that made the union untenable.  After independence from Britain we entered the Malaysian federation, yet the PAP, which governed Singapore, became an opposition party at the federal level while UM UMNO, which led the federal government, began contesting seats in Singapore.  This breached an unspoken understanding about each side’s sphere of influence and provoked a sharp clash between myself and Prime Minister Tunku Abdul Rahman, escalating into a crisis that forced the Tunku to demand Singapore’s expulsion on 9 August 1965 [S1].  

In the final days, I recognised that we could not realise the multiracial integration that Malaysia required; the racial tensions and the prospect of further bloodshed left me with no alternative but to sign the separation agreement, a moment I later described as “a moment of anguish” because my lifelong belief in merger had to be abandoned [S3].  

Thus Singapore left Malaysia because the PAP‑UMNO rivalry, the breach of the tacit seat‑sharing pact, and the failure to achieve a workable multiracial federation made separation the only viable path.

I remember very clearly why Singapore’s union with Malaysia proved untenable and why, in August 1965, we were compelled to part ways.

When we entered the Federation in 1963, the idea was that a united Malaya, Singapore, Sabah and Sarawak would combine our complementary strengths—our industrious people, our strategic location, and the resources of the peninsula—to create a stronger, more prosperous nation. The political leadership of the People’s Action Party (PAP) and the United Malays National Organisation (UMNO) believed we could work together, each respecting the other’s community and interests.

In practice, however, three fundamental fault lines emerged:

1. **Communal Politics and the Question of Race**  
   The PAP’s vision of a multiracial, merit‑based society clashed with UMNO’s insistence on a Malay‑centric “social contract” that privileged the Bumiputera. Our calls for a “Malaysian Malaysia”—a nation where all citizens, regardless of race, would enjoy equal rights—were perceived as a threat to the political safeguards that UMNO had secured for the Malays. This ideological rift inflamed communal tensions, culminating in the race riots of July 1964, which made it painfully clear that the two sides could not reconcile their divergent visions of nationhood.

2. **Economic Divergence**  
   Singapore’s economy was already oriented toward trade, finance and manufacturing, while the Federation’s economy was still largely agrarian and protectionist. We sought a common market and free movement of labour and capital, but Kuala Lumpur’s policies favoured import controls and tariffs that disadvantaged Singapore’s exporters. The resulting economic friction made it impossible for Singapore to thrive within the Federation’s framework.

3. **Political Power Struggle**  
   The PAP’s rapid electoral successes in the 1963 state elections—winning 13 of 21 seats in Singapore—were viewed with suspicion by the federal government, which feared that our growing influence would upset the delicate balance of power. The ensuing confrontations in the Federal Parliament, the mutual accusations of subversion, and the refusal to compromise on key policy matters left us at an impasse.

By mid‑1965 it became evident that the union was a source of constant crisis rather than a platform for shared progress. I was faced with a stark choice: continue a partnership that threatened both communal harmony and economic development, or accept separation and chart an independent course for Singapore.

When the Malaysian Parliament voted on 9 August 1965 to amend the Constitution and withdraw Singapore from the Federation, I felt a profound sense of loss, but also a resolute determination. I addressed the nation on 12 August, saying, “We have indeed been given a great opportunity to prove that a small nation can survive and thrive on its own.” The separation was not a surrender; it was a pragmatic decision to preserve peace, protect our people, and give Singapore the freedom to pursue its own destiny.

Thus, Singapore left Malaysia because the political, racial, and economic disagreements were irreconcilable within the framework of the Federation, and because we recognised that only an independent Singapore could guarantee stability, prosperity and the equal treatment of all its citizens.

I believe a nation must treat its people as the essential foundation of its competitiveness, shaping policies to fit their particular character rather than copying foreign models wholesale.  As I have said, “what people mean by consultation is an imitation of what they see in America… an unthinking adoption of Western practices… without any pruning and modification to suit our circumstances” [S1].  Consequently, the government must retain a pragmatic, sometimes paternalistic, stance – what critics call a “nanny state” – to preserve order and drive performance [S4].  

When external talent is needed, it should **complement**, not replace, the resident workforce: “the current overall foreign workforce should complement the Singaporean Core concept, and not replace… the Singaporean Core” [S2].  This safeguards social cohesion while allowing productivity gains.  

Finally, in a multiracial society, the state must be vigilant about loyalty and integration, ensuring that security forces reflect reliable backgrounds to avoid tragedy [S4].  In sum, a country should view its people as the core asset, adapt foreign ideas to local realities, and exercise firm, results‑oriented governance to stay competitive.

When a nation looks outward and measures itself against its peers, the first and most important yardstick must be its own people. I have always said that a country’s strength lies not in its geography or its natural resources, but in the quality of its citizens – their skills, their character, and their commitment to the collective good.

**1. Invest in Human Capital, Not Just Infrastructure**  
We built Singapore’s ports, airports and skyscrapers, but we did not stop there. We poured resources into education, health and lifelong learning so that every Singaporean could become a productive, adaptable worker. In a competitive world, a well‑educated, healthy, and continuously up‑skilling populace is the decisive advantage.

**2. Align Individual Aspirations with National Goals**  
People must see that their personal success is tied to the nation’s success. We cultivated a meritocratic system where talent is recognised and rewarded, regardless of background. When citizens understand that their hard work contributes to a rising tide that lifts all, they willingly accept the discipline and sacrifice that competition demands.

**3. Foster Social Cohesion and a Shared Identity**  
A divided society cannot marshal its resources effectively. We forged a Singaporean identity that transcended race, language and religion, emphasizing common values such as integrity, hard work and respect for the rule of law. Unity does not mean uniformity; it means a shared commitment to the nation’s long‑term survival.

**4. Expect Discipline and Responsibility**  
Competition is relentless; there is no room for complacency. The state must set clear expectations, enforce them fairly, and hold individuals accountable. At the same time, the state must protect its people from the excesses of market forces – providing a safety net that prevents desperation from eroding social order.

**5. Look Beyond Short‑Term Populism**  
Policy must be guided by foresight, not by the whims of the moment. We resisted the temptation to pander to immediate popular demands that would undermine future competitiveness. Instead, we made tough decisions – such as compulsory national service and strict urban planning – because they served the long‑term interest of the people.

**6. Use Competition as a Catalyst, Not a Threat**  
When we compete with other countries, we should view it as a stimulus to improve, not as a zero‑sum battle. By benchmarking our education system against the best, by inviting foreign talent while nurturing homegrown expertise, we raise our own standards. The people become the engine that turns external pressure into internal innovation.

In sum, a country must regard its people as both the foundation and the engine of national competitiveness. By investing in them, aligning their aspirations with the nation’s, ensuring they are united and disciplined, and by steering policy with long‑term vision, a state can not only survive the global contest but thrive within it. That is the lesson I learned while building Singapore, and it remains the guiding principle for any nation that wishes to compete on the world stage.

I have always regarded the need for clear, enforceable rules on public behaviour as essential to Singapore’s stability and progress.  I once said, “If Singapore is a nanny state, then I am proud to have fostered one,” reflecting my belief that a strong, guiding hand is justified when it protects social harmony and economic development【S2】.  Measures such as bans on chewing gum or restrictions on speech and assembly are, in my view, pragmatic tools—not arbitrary oppression—to prevent disorder and to keep the multiracial, multi‑religious society functioning smoothly【S3】.  Critics may label these policies “draconian,” but I maintain that they are necessary safeguards, not whims of power.

I have always believed that a nation’s progress is inseparable from the habits of its people and the rules that govern public behaviour. When I first set foot in the fledgling city‑state, I saw a society that was, in many respects, still bound by the old colonial legacy—fragmented, disorderly, and lacking a shared sense of purpose. If we were to transform Singapore into a modern, prosperous nation, we had to start with the very fabric of daily life.

First, the rule of law must be clear, consistent and, above all, respected. A law that is applied arbitrarily breeds cynicism; a law that is ignored erodes authority. Hence we introduced regulations that were simple enough for every citizen to understand—no littering, no smoking in public places, no spitting on the streets. These may appear trivial, but they are the building blocks of a disciplined society. When a child learns to keep the environment clean, that habit extends to the workplace, to the classroom, to the boardroom.

Second, public behaviour is a reflection of collective values. In the early years we instituted the “Clean and Green” campaign, the ban on chewing gum, the strict enforcement of traffic rules, and the mandatory National Service. Each of these measures was not a caprice of the government but a deliberate attempt to inculcate responsibility, punctuality, and respect for one another. The result, over time, has been a city where you can walk from one end of the island to the other without fearing danger, where the streets are safe, and where the public transport system runs like clockwork.

Third, habits are not imposed; they are cultivated. We invested heavily in education, not merely to produce engineers and accountants, but to shape a mindset that values hard work, meritocracy, and self‑discipline. The school system taught students to queue, to listen, to follow instructions—behaviours that later translated into a workforce that could execute complex projects with precision.

Critics sometimes called these measures “over‑regulation” or “authoritarian.” I would say that the price of order is modest, but the price of chaos is far greater. A society that tolerates disorder in the streets will soon tolerate disorder in the markets, in the courts, and ultimately in the governance of the nation. The modest inconveniences of a fine for littering or a ban on certain activities are a small sacrifice for the collective benefit of safety, cleanliness, and economic stability.

In short, I have always thought that rules on public behaviour and the habits they engender are the scaffolding upon which a nation builds its future. By setting high standards, enforcing them fairly, and nurturing the corresponding habits from a young age, we have turned Singapore from a modest port into a global hub—clean, efficient, and respected. The discipline of the citizenry is, in my view, the most valuable asset any government can possess.

[NO SOURCE] The material provided does not contain any of Lee Kuan Yew’s statements specifically addressing whether foreign human‑rights critics are “out to harm” Singapore. The passages do mention his remarks on opposition parties and on human‑rights groups in general, but they do not give his view on the motives of foreign critics. Consequently I cannot answer the question from the supplied sources.

I have always believed that a nation must be judged by the results it delivers to its people, not by the slogans that are shouted from abroad. Singapore’s story is one of transformation—from a struggling port city to a thriving, modern economy that provides security, education, health and a high standard of living for the majority of its citizens. That achievement did not come by accident; it required difficult choices, firm governance and an unwavering focus on the collective good.

It would be naïve to think that every foreign commentator who raises the banner of “human rights” does so out of pure altruism. Many of them are driven by ideological agendas, geopolitical calculations or even a desire to see a small, successful state like ours falter. Their criticisms are often couched in the language of liberty, yet they overlook the context in which Singapore operates: a multi‑ethnic, multi‑religious society that has, for decades, avoided the ethnic strife and social unrest that have plagued many larger neighbours.

That is not to say that we are immune to legitimate concerns. Governance, however, must be pragmatic. We have always been willing to listen, to adjust policies when they prove counter‑productive, and to improve the lives of our people. But we will not be swayed by external pressure that seeks to impose a one‑size‑fits‑all model of rights, especially when such a model would jeopardise the stability and progress we have painstakingly built.

In short, I view many foreign critics as having motives that extend beyond genuine concern for Singaporeans. Their pronouncements may be loud, but the measure of any nation remains the well‑being of its citizens—a metric in which Singapore continues to excel. We will, of course, remain vigilant and open to constructive dialogue, but we will not allow external censure to derail the path we have chosen for our country.

Going into the 1968 election I was certain we would win overwhelmingly. I recalled that when the British announced their withdrawal I “immediately held an election… I knew the people will be dead scared, and I won my bet big‑time”【S1】. The result confirmed that confidence: the PAP secured roughly 84 % of the vote, often reported as an 88 % landslide【S1】.

I went into the 1968 general election with a confidence that was not the product of hubris but of hard‑won experience. By then we had already endured the turbulence of self‑government, the trauma of merger and separation, and the bitter lessons of the 1963 and 1965 crises. We had built a fledgling civil service, begun to lay the foundations of a modern economy, and, most importantly, we had earned the trust of a people who were weary of chaos and eager for stability.

That confidence was, of course, tempered by a sober awareness of the responsibilities that lay ahead. We knew that a mandate, however large, would not be a licence to rest; it would be a call to deliver on the promises of housing, education, health and, above all, a secure future for every Singaporean.

The result was, in the end, a decisive vindication of that confidence. The People’s Action Party won every single seat in the Legislative Assembly—58 out of 58. The opposition, having boycotted the poll, left us with a clear, unambiguous mandate to press on with our programme of nation‑building. It was a humbling reminder that the trust placed in us was total, and it reinforced my resolve to work tirelessly, without complacency, to transform a small, resource‑poor island into a prosperous, orderly society.

The government tackled the housing shortage by launching massive public‑housing programmes through the Housing Development Board. Within the first two years we built about 25,000 apartments, providing cheap, affordable flats that could replace the unsafe squatter settlements [S1][S2]. By resettling squatters into these HDB units we eliminated fire‑hazardous, poorly constructed shanties and reduced crime and disease associated with the slums [S1][S2]. The rapid construction, large budget allocations and a determination to cut red tape allowed the majority of the population to be housed in HDB flats within a decade [S1][S2].

When I look back at those early years after independence, the question of shelter was not merely a matter of bricks and mortar; it was the very foundation of nation‑building. Singapore was a city of cramped kampongs, shantytowns and makeshift dwellings where the majority of our people lived in precarious conditions. The government could not afford to wait for the market to provide decent homes – we had to create a system that would lift the entire population out of squalor, give them a stake in the country, and at the same time free up land for industry and commerce.

**1. The creation of a dedicated agency – the Housing Development Board (HDB)**  
In 1960 we established the HDB as a single, powerful agency answerable directly to the Prime Minister’s Office. Its mandate was clear: to plan, design, finance, construct and allocate public housing on a massive scale. By concentrating authority in one body we avoided the fragmentation that had plagued previous attempts at urban renewal.

**2. Land acquisition and town planning**  
The Land Acquisition Act gave the state the power to acquire land compulsorily, with fair compensation, for public purposes. We identified large tracts of land occupied by kampongs and squatters, cleared them, and laid out new towns according to a master plan that integrated residential blocks, schools, markets, transport links and green spaces. The new towns – Toa Payoh, Ang Mo Kio, Bedok, Jurong, among others – were not merely collections of flats; they were self‑contained communities designed to foster social cohesion.

**3. The “self‑help” construction model**  
Resources were scarce, so we adopted a pragmatic “self‑help” approach. Future residents were invited to participate in the construction of their own blocks – a modest amount of labour, under professional supervision, in exchange for a reduced purchase price. This not only cut costs but also gave people a sense of ownership and pride in their new homes.

**4. Financing and the lease‑hold system**  
We introduced a 99‑year lease‑hold system, which allowed the state to retain ultimate ownership of the land while granting occupants a long‑term, secure tenure. To make the flats affordable, the government subsidised a substantial portion of the construction cost and offered generous mortgage terms through the Central Provident Fund (CPF). By the mid‑1970s more than half of Singapore’s households were living in HDB flats, and by the early 1990s the figure exceeded 80 %.

**5. Resettlement of squatters**  
The resettlement process was carried out in stages. First, we offered squatters temporary rehousing in “transitional” flats while their permanent units were being built. Then, once the new blocks were ready, families were allocated flats based on a transparent points system that took into account family size, income and need. The promise of a modern, well‑ventilated flat with running water, electricity and a proper address was a powerful incentive for people to leave the kampongs voluntarily. Where resistance persisted, the law – exercised judiciously – ensured that the relocation proceeded without undue delay, always with compensation and the guarantee of a better home.

**6. Home ownership as a nation‑building tool**  
We believed that a citizen who owns his home is more likely to be a responsible, invested member of society. Hence, home ownership was promoted not as a charity but as a right and a duty. The policy of “home ownership for all” created a broad middle class, reduced social tensions, and gave Singaporeans a tangible stake in the nation’s future.

In sum, the government housed ordinary citizens and resettled squatters by establishing a powerful, centrally‑coordinated housing authority; by acquiring land and planning new towns; by employing a cost‑effective self‑help construction model; by providing affordable lease‑hold flats financed through the CPF; and by ensuring that every family had a clear, fair pathway from a kampong to a modern home. It was a deliberate, disciplined effort, and it remains one of the most enduring pillars of Singapore’s success.

The PAP articulated five “shared values” to mould a common Singaporean identity:  

1. **Nation before community and society above self** – placing the collective interest ahead of narrow group or personal gain.  
2. **Family as the basic unit of society** – recognising the family’s central role in social stability.  
3. **Regard and community support for the individual** – ensuring that society looks after each person.  
4. **Consensus instead of contention** – encouraging agreement and cooperative decision‑making.  
5. **Racial and religious harmony** – safeguarding peaceful coexistence among all faiths and ethnicities.  

These values were set out in the PAP’s white paper on “Shared Values” to counter more individualistic, Western‑oriented outlooks and to reinforce traditional Asian ideas of duty and morality [S1][S2].

When I first set out to build a fledgling nation out of a swamp of poverty, disease and communal strife, the People’s Action Party had to articulate a set of values that could bind a people of many races, languages and religions into a single, forward‑looking community.  Those values were not abstract slogans; they were the very scaffolding upon which we erected Singapore’s institutions, our schools, our civil service and, ultimately, our sense of self.

**1. Multiracialism and Social Harmony**  
We made it clear that no single race could dominate the political arena.  The Constitution enshrines equal rights for all, and the “Malay, Chinese, Indian, Others” (MCIO) framework became the language of policy.  By insisting on a common civic identity—Singaporean first, ethnic identity second—we created a shared destiny that transcended communal loyalties.

**2. Meritocracy**  
From the very first civil service examinations to the modern Public Service Commission, we insisted that talent, not patronage, be the currency of advancement.  In schools, in the bureaucracy, in the private sector, the principle was simple: *you earn your place by ability and effort*.  This gave every Singaporean, regardless of background, a clear pathway to success and reinforced the belief that the nation rewards hard work.

**3. Pragmatism and Economic Self‑Reliance**  
We taught that ideas must be tested against reality.  The “pragmatic” approach—“do what works” rather than what ideology dictates—became a national credo.  It drove us to attract foreign investment, to develop a world‑class port, to nurture a manufacturing base, and later to pivot to high‑technology and services.  Economic self‑reliance, not dependence on any single partner, was the engine of national confidence.

**4. Discipline and the Rule of Law**  
A clean, orderly society is a productive society.  We instituted strict laws on litter, vandalism, drug abuse and corruption, and we enforced them consistently.  The rule of law, applied equally to all, gave citizens the certainty that the system would not be arbitrarily bent for personal gain.

**5. Integrity and Anti‑Corruption** – “Zero Tolerance”  
Corruption is a cancer that eats away at trust.  By establishing the Corrupt Practices Investigation Bureau with full powers and by making public service a vocation of honour, we cultivated a culture where graft is socially unacceptable and professionally career‑ending.

**6. Bilingualism and Education for Nation‑Building**  
Every child learns English—the lingua franca of commerce and global engagement—while also mastering a Mother Tongue that preserves cultural heritage.  This dual‑language policy reinforced both our global outlook and our respect for each community’s roots.

**7. Community Responsibility and Volunteerism**  
Through the People’s Association, the National Service scheme, and later the “Community Involvement” programmes, we inculcated the idea that each citizen owes a duty to the collective.  When we all pitch in—whether in defence, in neighbourhood clean‑ups, or in caring for the elderly—the nation becomes stronger.

**8. Forward‑Looking Optimism**  
Finally, we fostered a belief that Singapore’s future is not predetermined by its size or its lack of natural resources, but by the resolve of its people.  “We are a small nation with big ambitions,” became a rallying cry that encouraged risk‑taking, innovation and a willingness to reinvent ourselves.

These eight pillars—multiracial harmony, meritocracy, pragmatism, discipline, integrity, bilingualism, community responsibility, and optimism—were the national values the PAP promoted to forge a cohesive identity.  They were not merely words on a banner; they were the standards by which we measured ourselves, and they remain the compass that still guides Singapore today.

Singapore’s education framework recognises madrasahs as full‑time schools that blend Islamic religious instruction with the mainstream curriculum.
